topic: The Cambrian explosion was a burst of evolution starting about 538.8 million years ago, when most major animal groups (phyla) appear in the fossil record.
It lasted about 13–25 million years and produced animals with hard parts, eyes and complex bodies.
Its causes are debated: rising oxygen, new genes for body plans, and an arms race between predators and prey.
Fossil beds such as the Burgess Shale and Chengjiang preserve its soft-bodied animals.

Dating the Cambrian: William Buckland noticed the sudden appearance of fossils in the oldest Cambrian rocks in the 1840s.
Darwin saw the lack of earlier fossils as a serious difficulty for his theory in 'On the Origin of Species' (1859).
Radiometric dating puts the start of the Cambrian at about 538.8 million years ago.
Body fossils: Body fossils are the most informative evidence, but fossilisation is rare and the record is incomplete.
Exceptional deposits ('Lagerstätten') such as the Burgess Shale in Canada and Chengjiang in China preserve soft tissues.
Small shelly fossils, tiny tubes and plates, are among the earliest Cambrian fossils.
Trace fossils: Trace fossils are tracks, burrows and feeding marks.
They record soft-bodied animals and their behaviour, often before body fossils of the animals that made them.
Burrows become deeper and more complex at the start of the Cambrian.
Geochemical observations: Chemical markers show sharp changes in the environment around the start of the Cambrian.
Changes in carbon isotope ratios may reflect a mass extinction or a release of methane.
They may be a cause of the explosion, or a result of new biological activity.
Phylogenetic techniques: Cladistics builds family trees by grouping organisms that share derived traits.
Molecular clocks estimate when groups split from differences in their DNA.
Molecular clocks suggest many animal lineages split long before the Cambrian, earlier than the fossils show.
Explanation of key scientific terms: A phylum is a major grouping of animals by basic body plan, such as arthropods, molluscs or chordates.
A stem group consists of extinct relatives of a living group that lack some of its features.
Bilaterians have left–right symmetry and three tissue layers (triploblastic); coelomates have a body cavity.
Precambrian life: Stromatolites, built by microbial mats, declined after about 1.25 billion years ago, possibly due to grazing animals.
The Ediacaran biota (about 575–539 million years ago) were large, soft-bodied organisms, many unlike any living animal.
Some Ediacaran forms, such as Kimberella, may be early animals.
Cambrian life: Burrowing, shells and skeletons appear at the start of the Cambrian.
Trilobites appear about 521 million years ago and became one of the most successful Cambrian groups.
Burgess Shale animals such as Anomalocaris, Opabinia and Wiwaxia show a great variety of body plans.
Early chordates, including the first vertebrates, appear in Chengjiang.
Stages: The fastest diversification came in the first 20–25 million years of the Cambrian.
It ended around the base of Cambrian Series 2, 521 million years ago, when the first trilobites appear.
Authors divide the interval differently, depending on which fossils they emphasise.
Validity: Some animal groups, such as sponges and cnidarians, existed before the Cambrian.
Part of the 'explosion' may reflect better preservation of hard parts rather than a true burst of evolution.
Survivorship bias also matters: groups that survived to today look as if they appeared suddenly.
Possible causes: Environmental: rising oxygen levels, an ozone layer, the end of the Snowball Earth glaciations, and more calcium in seawater.
Developmental: the evolution of Hox genes and other genetic tool-kits for building complex bodies.
Ecological: predators and prey in an arms race, eyes, burrowing, and empty niches after the end-Ediacaran extinction.
Relationship with the Great Ordovician B: After an extinction at the end of the Cambrian, a second radiation followed: the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event.
It established the groups that dominated the rest of the Paleozoic.
Some studies see the two as one long radiation.
Uniqueness of the early Cambrian biodive: The rate of evolution in the early Cambrian is unmatched among marine animals.
It may have come in two waves: first on the Ediacaran sea floor, then into the open water.
No new phyla have appeared since; later radiations only varied existing body plans.
